'''''Bromus hordeaceus''''', the '''soft brome''', is an [[Annual plant|annual]] or [[Biennial plant|biennial]] species of grass in the grass family ([[Poaceae]]). It is also known in North America as '''bull grass''', '''soft cheat''', and '''soft chess'''.

It is the most common species of ''[[Bromus]]'' in Britain, where it can be found on roadsides, waste ground, meadows, and cultivated land. It is found throughout Europe and western Asia, and was [[introduced species|introduced]] into North and South America and Australia.

==Taxonomy==
Previously known as ''[[species:Bromus mollis|B. mollis]]'',<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.kew.org/data/grasses-db/www/imp01633.htm|title=RBG Kew: GrassBase - Bromus hordeaceus Description|last=kh02kg|date=|website=www.kew.org|language=en-GB|access-date=2018-02-27}}</ref> this species belongs to a group of closely related species, including some hybrids, which are difficult to tell apart. Some of the other species in this group include: ''B. thominii, B. lepidus, B. ferronii,'' and ''B. molliformis''.<ref>Hubbard, C. E. ''Grasses''. Penguin Books. 1978.</ref>

==Description==
The plant is pubescent entirely and lacks [[rhizome]]s. It can grow {{convert|7-110|cm|0|abbr=on}} high, sometimes in tufts, sometimes singly.

The smooth, yellowish brown [[Culm (botany)|culm]]s measure {{convert|0.5-5|mm|2|abbr=on}} wide at their base, and are minutely to densely pubescent, with hairs measuring up to {{convert|0.6|mm|2|abbr=on}} long. The moderately to densely pilose [[leaf sheath]]s are mostly closed, with hairs {{convert|1.2|mm|abbr=on}} long. The plant lacks [[Auricle (botany)|auricle]]s. The membraneous and erose [[ligule]]s are {{convert|1-2.6|mm|2|abbr=on}} long and are glabrous or pubescent. The grey-green leaf blades are {{convert|2.2-18|cm|1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1-5.3|mm|2|abbr=on}} wide, with a pubescent adaxial surface and an abaxial surface pubescent with hairs about one quarter the length of those on the adaxial surface. The leaf margins are smooth or serrated.

The grey-green to purple [[panicle]]s are {{convert|2.5-14|cm|1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1-4|cm|2|abbr=on}} wide. The panicles can be dense or reduced to just one spikelet. The erect to ascending or lax branches of the panicle are scabrous or pubescent, each branch bearing one spikelet.

The ovate-lanceolate [[spikelet]]s are {{convert|1.7-3|cm|2|abbr=on}}, including the [[Awn (botany)|awns]] {{convert|3-8|mm|abbr=on}} long.<ref>Edgar E. & Connor H.E. (2000). ''Flora of New Zealand, Vol. V, Grasses''. Manaaki Whenua Press, Lincoln, New Zealand. p. 362-3</ref> The [[Rachilla (floral axis)|rachilla]]e can be visible when the spikelet is mature and the spikelet has six to eleven florets. The subequal [[glume]]s are minutely to densely pubescent and the keels are serrated. The lower glumes are {{convert|5.2-7|mm|2|abbr=on}} long with three to five nerved, and the upper glumes are {{convert|6-8.5|mm|2|abbr=on}} long and seven- to nine-nerved. The [[Lemma (botany)|lemma]]s are {{convert|7.5-9|mm|1|abbr=on}} long and {{convert|1.9-2.5|mm|2|abbr=on}} wide, with seven to nine visible, conspicuous nerves. The lemmas have hyaline margins {{convert|0.3-0.6|mm|3|abbr=on}} broad. The apex is bifid and the cleft is {{convert|0.3-0.7|mm|3|abbr=on}} deep. The awns are {{convert|4-7.6|mm|2|abbr=on}} long, arising {{convert|0.4-1.2|mm|abbr=on}} below the lemma. The [[Palea (botany)|palea]]s are shorter than the lemmas, with glabrous backs and ciliate keels. The dark brown [[anther]]s are {{convert|0.3-1.3|mm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=Texas>{{cite book |pages= 335–337 |url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/41650331#page/347/mode/1up |title= Journal of the Botanical Research Institute of Texas |volume= 1 |number= 1 |publisher= Fort Worth, Texas: Botanical Research Institute of Texas |author= Botanical Research Institute of Texas |year= 2007}}</ref>

It grows during winter and flowers from late spring onwards, maturing in the summer.<ref name=Dastgheib>Dastgheib F. & Poole N.  (2010). Seed biology of brome grass weeds (Bromus diandrus and B. hordeaceus) and effects of land management, “New Zealand Plant Protection” 63: 78-83</ref> The grass blooms in May and August.<ref>{{Calflora|Bromus hordeaceus}}</ref>

''Bromus hordeaceus'' is closely related to and difficult to distinguish from ''[[Bromus racemosus]]''. The only obvious distinguishing characteristic is the level of lemma nerve protrusion; the lemma nerves are raised and conspicuous in ''B. hordeaceus'' while they are smooth and obscure in ''B. racemosus''.<ref name=Texas/>

==Distribution and habitat==
''Bromus hordeaceus'' is native to the [[Mediterranean]] basin, and is now widely distributed across North America, Europe, Africa, and Australia. It grows in waste areas, road verges, fields, grassy plains, and sandy beaches.<ref name=Texas/> The grass prefers drained or dry soils consisting of clay loam or sand, especially areas tending to be less fertile. The plant is resistant to drought and temperature variations.<ref name=CRC>{{cite book |page= 375 |url= https://books.google.com/books?id=8ieqQs7hIREC&q=Bromus+hordeaceus&pg=PA375 |title= CRC World Dictionary of Grasses: Common Names, Scientific Names, Eponyms, Synonyms, and Etymology |author= Umberto Quattrocchi |publisher= CRC Press |year= 2006 |isbn= 9781420003222}}</ref>

==Invasive species==
''Bromus hordeaceus'' can be a weed in cereal crops. It grows in wheat and spring barley crops competing and reducing their yield. The seeds can contaminate the crop seeds and lower seed quality.<ref name=Dastgheib />

There are very few herbicides that selectively control soft brome in wheat or barley. The management of this weed is mostly based on an integrated programme. This includes hygiene to minimise its introduction to the fields as well as cleaning the fence lines where the infestation is more severe. A good crop rotation is useful as ''B. hordeaceus'' can be controlled with several herbicides in most other crops in the rotation. Growers in New Zealand use stubble burning to reduce the seed input in the following crops.<ref name=Dastgheib />

==Subspecies==
''Bromus hordeaceus'' subsp. ''ferronii'', the least soft brome, is a rare annual that occurs in northwestern Europe. The grass is tufted and erect or decumbent. The spikelets are villous and the awns are spreading or twisted. This subspecies can be used for erosion control.<ref name=CRC/>

''Bromus hordeaceus'' subsp. ''hordeaceus'', the soft brome or soft chess, is an annual or biennial occurring in Europe, western North America, and northeastern North America. The culms are {{convert|10-70|cm|abbr=on}} tall. The subspecies lacks auricles and the ligules are hyaline and smooth. The panicles are {{convert|5-10|cm|abbr=on}} long. The spikelets are cleistogamous. The lemmas are {{convert|8-11|mm|abbr=on}} long.<ref name=North>{{cite book |page= 232 |title= Flora of North America: North of Mexico |volume= 24 |author= Flora of North America Editorial Committee |publisher= Oxford University Press |year= 1993 |isbn= 9780195310719}}</ref> The apex of the ovary is pubescent. This subspecies is primarily a forage plant, and occurs in waste places and roadsides.<ref name=CRC/> The subspecies has a [[diploid number]] of 14 or 28.<ref name=Rhod>{{cite journal |page= 111 |url= https://www.biodiversitylibrary.org/page/33041860#page/117/mode/1up |title= Atlas of the flora of New England: Poaceae |journal= Rhodora |volume= 100 |publisher= New England Botanical Club |author= Angelo, R. and Boufford, David Edward |year= 1998}}</ref>

''Bromus hordeaceus'' subsp. ''molliformis'' is a tufted annual occurring in France, Italy, California, Idaho, and New Mexico. The culms are {{convert|15-25|cm|abbr=on}} tall. The subspecies has a contracted panicle about {{convert|10|cm|abbr=on}} long, with villous spikelets. The pubescent lemmas are {{convert|8-11|mm|abbr=on}} long and have rounded margins.<ref name=North/> The scabrid awns are somewhat erect. The subspecies grows as a weed in cultivated areas, typically in dry soils but rarely in wetlands.<ref name=CRC/>

''Bromus hordeaceus'' subsp. ''pseudothominii'' occurs in Europe and sporadically throughout North America. The culms are {{convert|10-70|cm|abbr=on}} tall. The panicles are up to {{convert|10|cm|abbr=on}} long. The typically glabrous lemmas are {{convert|6.5-8|mm|abbr=on}} long. The awns are straight and erect. The subspecies can be mistaken for ''[[Bromus lepidus]]'' in its similar lemma form and characteristics.<ref name=North/> It grows in meadows and grasslands.<ref name=CRC/>

''Bromus hordeaceus'' subsp. ''thominei'', the lesser soft brome, occurs in West Europe and the western United States, in California and the Pacific coast of Canada. The culms are {{convert|2-16|cm|abbr=on}} long. The panicles are {{convert|1-3|cm|abbr=on}} long and often consist of a single spikelet. The pubescent or glabrous lemmas are {{convert|6.5-7.5|mm|abbr=on}} long, with bluntly angled margins. The awns can become [[divaricate]] when mature.<ref name=North/> The subspecies grows in waste areas and sandy soils or dunes.<ref name=CRC/> The subspecies has a diploid number of 28.<ref name=Rhod/>
